newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong probes inferno, welding suspected, toll 37.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong probes inferno, welding suspected, toll 37.

text.p: Hong Kong probed the reasons for the territory's worst building blaze on record on Friday after a raging inferno, believed to have been caused by welding work, killed 37 people in the "golden mile" tourist district.
Police removed bodies from the charred wreckage of the gutted Garley Building on Nathan Road on the Kowloon peninsula and forensic detectives scoured the 16-storey hulk for clues.
The fire raged for 21 hours on Wednesday and Thursday, and was the worst high-rise blaze in the British colony's one and a half centuries-long history in terms of death toll and damage.
Police on Friday revised the death toll down to 37 from 39 after comparing the number of bodies found with reports of people believed missing.

And one day after conquering the blaze, firefighters were battling another serious fire in a plastics factory on the 14th floor of a building in the Causeway Bay district. No casualties were reported.

After visiting Nathan Road, where hundreds of anguished kin waited night and day for news of missing loved-ones, colonial Governor Chris Patten was himself choking back the tears as he announced inquiry plans in the Legislative Council on Thursday.

The disaster dramatically spotlighted crowded Hong Kong's notoriously shoddy fire safety situation -- weak rules and a lax fire consciousness. Some 700 office blocks of a 20-year-plus vintage, standing shoulder to shoulder in densely packed districts, are potential deathtraps for their lack of sprinklers, alarm systems, fire fighting equipment and emergency plans, according to experts.

Patten told legislators that fire service experts would conduct an immediate investigation into the blaze, and that he would consider setting up a special commission of inquiry after he studies their findings in two weeks time.
"We must also make absolutely sure we learn all the lessons from this tragedy and do everything we can to minimise the risk of it ever happening again," he said.
He pledged to review the scope of a new draft bill on fire safety to see whether it should be extended to cover older buildings that are currently beyond its reach.
Such a move has been firmly resisted by lobbyists for the cost-conscious building industry in past debates on the issue.

Fire services director Peter Cheung said sparks from a welder's blowtorch were believed to have ignited combustible materials in an elevator shaft on the ground floor, which housed a Chinese arts and crafts emporium.
The blaze rapidly engulfed the lower floors then shot up the shaft and gutted the three top storeys, where 22 people trapped in an office were killed on one floor alone.
"We have learned there was a single source of the fire within the lift shaft on the ground floor," Cheung said.
The welders, who are on the list of missing, were repairing the lift and had posted a notice telling people not to worry about a burning smell because it was just blowtorches.
The fire service was stunned by the speed of the blaze. "In 25 years of experience I haven't seen a fire spread so rapidly. It's speed was amazing," said senior fireman Kwok Jing-keung.

He said the fire was sucked up the lift shaft, which acted as a funnel for the rising flames, which then burst on to higher floors tearing through highly-flammable temporary plywood sheets that had been placed on the out-of-order lift doors by workers.
Grease on the lift cables and tracks aided the spread.
"The smoke accumulated at the top, got really hot, spread sideways -- what we call mushrooming," he said.
The drama was aggravated by escape routes between higher floors of the building being cut off, leaving nowhere to run.
For such buildings, fire insurance is not obligatory in Hong Kong. Owners can decide for themselves whether to buy cover.
No figures were yet available on the value of material damage caused in the Garley Building.
